lines: The last setting we looked at changed how an existing kind of value behaves.
This one is different. It's a kind of value that simply didn't exist before, built for data whose own shape isn't fixed.
Before it existed, holding that kind of data meant picking between two choices, and neither one was good.
Keep it as plain text, and the engine understands nothing about it. Force it into a fixed shape, and the moment one record doesn't match that shape, something breaks.
Here's a question worth sitting with before the answer comes.
Pull the same one piece out of a record, over and over, many times. Is that faster when the record is kept as plain text, or when it's kept in the new, purpose-built form?
steps.answer: The purpose-built form is faster. The plain text pays its parsing cost every single time; the other form only paid it once.

lines: Slower from plain text, and that's measured directly, not assumed.
Pulling the same piece out again and again costs real, meaningfully more time from plain text than from the purpose-built form, on the identical underlying data.
Here's why one stays fast where the other doesn't.

The new form carries its own description right alongside the value -- what kind of thing it is, where each named piece lives -- shared once across a whole column, not repeated record by record. Pulling a piece out becomes following a pointer, not reading text from the start.
Here's a different kind of question.

Take one piece of data that's sometimes a number and sometimes plain text, record by record, and force it into a column that only allows one of those. Does every single record make it through, or does one quietly vanish?
steps.answer: One vanishes. The record whose value doesn't match the column's one allowed type comes back as nothing at all.

lines: One vanishes, and that's measured directly too.
The record that doesn't match the fixed shape comes back as nothing. Read the same data through the new, purpose-built form instead, and every single record's actual value comes through untouched.
Here's why that happens.
A fixed shape has to commit to exactly one type for a field before a single record has even arrived. The moment real data disagrees with that early commitment, something has to be thrown away.
There's a way to get some of that fixed shape's own speed back, without going back to its brittleness.
Pull just the one piece that gets read constantly out into its own dedicated, fast column, and leave everything else exactly as tolerant as it was.

That particular trick arrived in a Spark release that comes after the one every other example in this chapter runs on, so it's named here from what Spark itself documents about it, not measured directly.
Three ways of holding the same kind of data, and each one pays its own cost somewhere different.
Plain text pays every single time it's read. A fixed shape pays once, up front, by risking what it might throw away.
The purpose-built form in between pays once too, but keeps everything -- at least until one piece of it needs to be made just as fast as the fixed shape.
